items.title: Ignacio Berroa interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 22, 2021 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: He recommended me with different musicians in New York, mainly those who went into the recording industry like Arturo Chico O’Farrill to name one of them.

ctx.x: And here you are, you’re in the country for about a year and can you tell me how all of a sudden you appear in a club as Dizzy Gillespie’s drummer?

Life is full of surprises. I arrived to New York and I got in touch with the Cuban musician Mario Bauza who was responsible for that Afro-Cuban jazz movement in the 40s it was Mario who told Dizzy to hire Chano Pozo and so forth and so on and the rest is history. So I met Mario. Mario became my mentor, it was Mario the guy that took me to the union musicians in New York. He recommended me with different musicians in New York, mainly those who went into the recording industry like Arturo Chico O’Farrill to name…

imagine all the drummers that Dizzy had on his phone book. So after calling everybody or I don’t know, whatever, and it turns out that everybody was busy, he remembered, oh Mario told me about a Cuban drummer. So he called Mario and Mario told him, “Let me see if the guy is available.” I was available and that’s how I ended up playing this night, six months after my arrival to the United States I was sitting behind Dizzy Gillespie on drums playing at a club in Manhattan called Fat Tuesday. It was pure luck I…
